05b4a1898b:
This chapter covers two decisions that sit on either side of every tool call.

2.2 is about what a tool says when it fails. The model has to tell a timeout from a policy refusal, a missing permission from an empty result, and act differently on each.

2.3 is about which tools each agent is allowed to see. Why do eighteen tools select worse than five? How do you give a subagent a narrow cross-role tool for the common case? And how does tool_choice turn "the model usually calls the right tool" into "this request will call a tool"?

Along the way the chapter traces the error vocabulary back through SMTP, HTTP, gRPC and Spring. It separates MCP protocol errors from tool execution errors, checked against the specification text. It builds an MCP server with structured errors. It measures tool-count effects with a simulation, and says what the simulation cannot tell you. Finally it states what tool_choice does and does not guarantee, including the model restrictions the docs list. Python and Java/Spring.
ead5dd6d86: Reading time: 3.5 to 4 hours  ·  Companion code, 28 Python examples and 2 Java programs for this chapter: ccarf-companion/06-mcp-errors-tool-distribution/. Run bash run_all.sh. Every Python example works offline with --mock, and two optional examples run against the real model when a key is set.
f3dc45bc7d:
The chapter rests on two sentences.

A tool failure is information the model acts on, so it must say what kind of failure it was (transient, validation, business, permission), whether trying again can help, and what the model should say or do next; a uniform "operation failed", or a failure disguised as an empty success, removes the one fact the model needed and produces a wrong action with full confidence.

A tool list is the menu the model chooses from, so each agent should see only the four or five tools its role needs, plus at most a narrow cross-role tool for a frequent simple case, and tool_choice is the per-request lever that makes a tool call (any tool, or one named tool) mandatory when "the model usually does it" is not good enough.
bdfece9e91:
Everything else in the chapter follows from those two sentences.

The error vocabulary (errorCategory, isRetryable, customerMessage) exists because each kind of failure needs a different next step, and the model is the one choosing that step. An empty result and a failed search must never look alike, because a model treats an empty list as a fact about the world. Subagents recover locally because a failure that can be fixed one level down should cost the level above nothing.

The 2.3 side works the same way. Scoping exists because every tool definition is text the model must weigh on every request, and every extra tool is one more way to be wrong. The scoped cross-role tool exists because a hub-and-spoke system pays latency for every trip through the hub. And tool_choice exists because probabilistic selection is the wrong guarantee for a step that must happen.
7db293a06c:
The official task statements list the items below, and each one is taught explicitly in this chapter.

For 2.2, the knowledge points are:

  • the MCP isError flag pattern for communicating tool failures to the agent;
  • the difference between transient errors (timeouts, service unavailability), validation errors (invalid input), business errors (policy violations) and permission errors;
  • that uniform error responses ("Operation failed") prevent the agent from making appropriate recovery decisions;
  • the difference between retryable and non-retryable errors, where returning non-retryable errors as retryable wastes calls.

The 2.2 skills: return structured error metadata (errorCategory, isRetryable, a human-readable description). Give customer-friendly explanations for non-retryable business errors. Recover locally inside subagents from transient failures, and propagate only what cannot be resolved, with what was attempted and any partial results. Distinguish access failures from valid empty results.

For 2.3, the knowledge points are:

  • giving an agent too many tools (the guide contrasts 18 with 4 or 5) degrades selection reliability by increasing decision complexity;
  • agents with tools outside their specialty tend to misuse them (a synthesis agent attempting web searches);
  • scoped tool access with a few limited cross-role tools is the remedy;
  • the tool_choice options "auto", "any" and forced selection {"type":"tool","name":"..."}.

The 2.3 skills: restrict each subagent's tool set to its role. Replace generic tools with constrained alternatives (fetch_url becomes load_document with URL validation). Give a scoped cross-role tool for a high-frequency need; the official sample puts verify_fact on the synthesis agent for the 85% simple case. Force a specific tool to run first, for example extract_metadata before enrichment. And use "any" to guarantee that some tool is called.
0d814025ce:
A Spring developer should keep two analogies in mind.

For errors, an agent is a client of your tool API. Does your API return an HTTP 500 with the body error for everything, or a ProblemDetail with a type a client can branch on? That question is the whole of 2.2.

For tool sets, each subagent is a service with an IAM role. Giving every service every permission "in case it needs it" fails here for the same reason it fails there: blast radius. And there's one new reason. Unneeded tools also lower the quality of the decisions the service makes.
190818bd9e:
Neither half of this chapter is new engineering. Classifying failures by what the caller should do next is about as old as networked software. Giving a component only the capabilities it needs is older still.

What is new is the caller. It's a language model, and it reads the failure as prose. Tracing the lineage shows which parts transfer unchanged (the categories, the retry rule, least privilege) and which do not (the reader).
348d947e27:
SMTP (RFC 821, 1982; RFC 5321 today) is the earliest clean example. Every reply is a three-digit code, and the first digit is a verdict on what to do:

  • 2yz success;
  • 4yz "transient negative completion": the action did not happen, but the condition is temporary, so try again later;
  • 5yz "permanent negative completion": do not repeat the request in the same form.

A mail server that gets 451 Requested action aborted: local error in processing queues the message and retries with backoff. One that gets 550 No such user bounces it to the sender. That one digit is the isRetryable flag, thirty years before anyone wrote the word "agent".

HTTP copied the idea into its status classes. 4xx says the client made a mistake and should change the request. 5xx says the server failed to fulfil a request that may have been fine. The convention stuck because it answers the only question a generic client can act on without understanding the application: should I repeat this, change it, or give up?
e18ae2a200:
The classes are coarse, and the coarseness is a lesson. 404 can mean "you mistyped the id" or "the thing was deleted and that is final". 409 can mean "retry after refreshing" or "this is forbidden by a rule". 503 can mean "retry in a second" or "down for the weekend".

So application protocols added a second layer: an application error code in the body, because the status class alone does not carry enough. SOAP faults (2000) did the same with faultcode and detail. Every generation rediscovers the same thing. A verdict (retry or not) and a reason (what, specifically) are separate pieces of information, and you need both.
f29086b054:
gRPC (open-sourced 2015) defined a closed set of 17 status codes (OK plus 16 errors). Its documentation tells the caller what to do with each:

  • INVALID_ARGUMENT means the argument is wrong whatever the state of the system;
  • FAILED_PRECONDITION means the system is not in a state where the operation can run, and the caller should not retry until the state is fixed;
  • UNAVAILABLE is the code for "retry with backoff";
  • PERMISSION_DENIED and UNAUTHENTICATED are separate because they need different remedies.

The doc comments on those codes are, in effect, the recovery policy. That is the standard the exam's four categories are built to meet.
be17de2c7f:
Your own world has the same split. Spring's data-access exception hierarchy divides DataAccessException into two branches:

  • TransientDataAccessException, including QueryTimeoutException and CannotAcquireLockException: "the operation might succeed if retried";
  • NonTransientDataAccessException, including DataIntegrityViolationException and PermissionDeniedDataAccessException: "retrying the same operation will fail the same way".

A Spring Retry or Resilience4j configuration that retries only on the transient branch is the same policy this chapter builds. It's just applied to a database instead of a tool.

For HTTP APIs, RFC 7807 (2016), replaced by RFC 9457 in 2023, standardised the error body as "problem details": type, title, status, detail, instance, plus extension members. Spring Framework 6 added ProblemDetail and ErrorResponse to model it. Section 12 maps this chapter's payload onto it.
07aa289ac4:
The Model Context Protocol (November 2024) is JSON-RPC 2.0 underneath. JSON-RPC has its own reserved error codes: -32700 parse error, -32600 invalid request, -32601 method not found, -32602 invalid params, -32603 internal error. Those describe failures of the message exchange.

MCP added a second route for failures of the work: a normal result with isError: true and content the model can read. The Claude API has the same idea on its own side, as the is_error field of a tool_result block (chapter 01).

The new element is the reader. A status-code consumer in 2015 was a program with a branch for each code. The consumer in 2026 reads the body as text and chooses among behaviours that nobody coded as branches. That makes the content of the body more important, not less. The status class is gone, so whatever the body says is all the verdict and all the reason there is. The Claude docs say it in one line: write instructive error messages, with what went wrong and what to try next, instead of "failed".
0ffbeb60fa:
Least privilege (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975) says every component should operate with the minimum set of capabilities it needs. Unix tools (1970s) made the same point as design: small programs that each do one job, composed by the caller. Service-oriented systems rediscovered it as bounded contexts and per-service credentials.

None of that was about choice quality. A service with too many permissions is a security problem. It does not get worse at deciding.

The new fact for agents is that the tool list is also part of the prompt, and the model chooses from it by reading. Retrieval work on tool use (Gorilla, 2023; ToolLLM, 2023) retrieved the relevant API documentation instead of listing thousands of APIs. A long list neither fits nor selects well.

Anthropic's engineering guidance on writing tools says "more tools don't always lead to better outcomes" and that "too many tools or overlapping tools can also distract agents". The tool search documentation says selection degrades once you exceed 30 to 50 available tools. It gives no source for the figure, so treat it as guidance, not a measured threshold. The exam's 18 versus 4 or 5 sits well below that. The claim is that decision quality starts to suffer long before the context fills up.
4504c2ad1f:
MCP has two ways to report that a tools/call went wrong. Exam answers and real servers both go wrong by mixing them up. The specification (the Tools page, section "Error Handling") puts it in two numbered items.

  • Protocol errors are standard JSON-RPC errors, for problems with the request itself: an unknown tool, a request that does not satisfy the CallToolRequest schema, a server error.
  • Tool execution errors are reported in the tool result with isError: true, for problems that happened while doing the work: API failures, input validation errors (the spec's example is a date in the wrong format or a value out of range) and business logic errors.

The spec gives the reason for the split in a sentence worth memorising. Tool execution errors "contain actionable feedback that language models can use to self-correct and retry with adjusted parameters". Protocol errors "indicate issues with the request structure itself that models are less likely to be able to fix". Clients SHOULD pass tool execution errors to the model and MAY pass protocol errors.
d7d69c1e8b: On the wire the two look like this. The first is a protocol error, the unknown-tool example from the spec. It is a JSON-RPC error member, there is no result, and the code is a JSON-RPC code. The second is a tool execution error: a perfectly ordinary result whose isError field is true.
45b135d226:
One detail in the spec's history is worth knowing, because it matches what servers actually do. The 2025-06-18 revision listed "invalid arguments" under protocol errors. The 2025-11-25 revision (and the current draft) moved it. "Input validation errors (e.g., date in wrong format, value out of range)" are now tool execution errors. The protocol-error list became unknown tools, malformed requests that fail the CallToolRequest schema, and server errors.

The reasoning is in the sentence above: a model can fix a date, but it cannot fix a malformed envelope. Your client library or server framework may predate the move. If so, it may still raise argument validation failures as JSON-RPC errors that your host never shows to the model, and the model repeats the bad call blind. Check which behaviour your SDK version has (example 01 prints it).
9d18460d6a:
Say Claude Code or the Agent SDK receives a tool result with isError: true from an MCP server. It puts the content into a tool_result block with is_error: true in the next request to the model. The loop in chapter 01 does the same by hand.

Nothing else happens. There is no retry layer inside the SDK, no category-aware behaviour, no special treatment of the words in the content.

The flag changes how the model reads the block. The Claude docs say a result flagged as an error is treated as a failed attempt. For invalid or missing parameters, they say Claude will retry two to three times with corrections before apologising to the user. Everything beyond that is decided by the content you wrote, including whether the model retries a timeout, explains a policy or escalates. The flag is the envelope. The payload is the message.
c3cae8a27c:
Most real servers don't build error results by hand. They raise exceptions and rely on the framework. What the framework does with those exceptions matters, and it differs by SDK version. Example 01 runs five failing calls through an in-process server on both SDK generations.

On mcp 2.x (where FastMCP became MCPServer), a tool that raises a bare RuntimeError yields an isError result whose text is only "Error executing tool crashes". The SDK withholds the exception text and logs the traceback server-side.

On 1.x the same call yields "Error executing tool crashes: psycopg2.OperationalError: could not connect to db-prod-7.internal:5432". That puts an internal hostname in the model's context, and possibly in the customer's reply.

Some things are the same in both versions. An argument that fails the schema ("two" for an int) comes back as an isError result carrying a pydantic validation message. An unknown tool name comes back as isError text "Unknown tool: no_such_tool", not as a JSON-RPC error.

So the SDK gives you the channel, but not the contract. 2.x is safe and uniform; 1.x is informative and leaky. Neither tells the model whether to retry. Section 11 builds the layer that does.
c0a85015f5:
To see why the content of an error decides the outcome, look at what the model has when the error arrives. Its context contains the system prompt, the conversation, its own earlier tool_use block, and now a tool_result flagged as an error, with some text.

That text is the only evidence about what happened. The model can't see the stack trace, the HTTP status, the timing, or the other callers hitting the same service. It produces its next step by predicting what a competent assistant would do, given that text.

If the text says "Operation failed", a competent assistant does what people do with an opaque failure. It tries again once or twice, then apologises and says the system is having problems. If the text says "Delivered 45 days ago; the refund window is 30 days", a competent assistant explains the window and offers an alternative.

The model is doing the right thing with each text. The difference in outcome comes entirely from what the tool chose to say.
46b7e39024:
Example 02 isolates this. It runs three failures through the same refund tool:

  • a business refusal (45 days, window 30);
  • a transient fault (the order service times out once);
  • a permission limit (799.00 against a 500.00 agent limit).

Each runs twice: once with the error flattened to "Operation failed", and once as the structured payload. A scripted reader plays the model. The blind reader sees only that something failed. The structured reader acts on the category.

These are stand-ins that encode the argument, not measurements of Claude. Example 27 runs the same experiment against the real model when you have a key. What the numbers show is how much of the outcome is fixed by the information, before any model quality enters.
fcaa033544:
Read the transient row first, because it's the one that makes uniform errors look acceptable. When the failure is a blip, retrying is the right move. So the blind reader gets the right answer by accident, and a team that tests only a timeout concludes that "Operation failed" is fine.

The damage is in the other two rows. The blind reader retries a policy refusal three times: three upstream hits for a call that can never succeed. Then it tells the customer the system is down. That's false, and the customer will act on it by calling back. The same flattening on the permission row sends the customer away from the only path that works, which is escalation to a supervisor.

Both wrong outcomes look like ordinary service problems in the logs. No exception, a handled error, a polite final message.
eb686431bd:
A model can go wrong in three distinct ways when the error carries too little, and the exam options are built from them.

  • Blind retry: it repeats a call that cannot succeed (a business or permission failure). That wastes calls and adds latency, and for side-effecting tools it can cause harm.
  • Premature surrender: it gives up on a call that a retry would have completed, because the error looks fatal.
  • Confabulated explanation: it needs to tell the customer something, has no facts, and fills the gap with plausible text. For example, it invents a policy to explain a refusal.

A uniform message invites all three, because the model must choose among them with no evidence. A structured error removes the guesswork for each. isRetryable and the category address the first two, and a ready-made customerMessage addresses the third.
89faf22054:
An error result is written into the model's context and read like any other text. It is not a control signal. Nothing guarantees the model will obey isRetryable: false.

It is strong, cheap evidence. In a system where it matters absolutely (never retry a payment), you enforce it in the harness as well (section 07), exactly as chapter 03 enforces prerequisites outside the prompt. Design the payload so the model usually does the right thing. Design the harness so it cannot do the wrong thing expensively.
f7fa80b192:
The exam names four categories. They're defined by what the caller should do next, not by what went wrong. That is why they survive translation between HTTP, gRPC, Spring and MCP: each one answers the same two questions.

Would this same call succeed if repeated later? If yes, the failure is transient. Would a call with corrected input succeed? If yes, it is a validation error. If neither, the request was understood and valid. The remaining reasons are that a rule forbids it (business) or that this caller is not entitled to it (permission).

Real systems need a fifth, internal, for failures that are the tool's own bug. These are not retryable by the model and not explainable to the customer. Don't dress them up as one of the four.
5abbbf0fc7: You don't have to invent the mapping; your services already have one. Example 03 prints the table below from the code the examples use. Treat it as a default that a human reviews. The status class alone does not decide, as the hard cases after it show.
f9bb69d42d:
The word "retryable" in the exam's isRetryable hides a distinction, and the companion payload makes it explicit. A transient error is retryable with the same input. A validation error is retryable with corrected input. Treat both as plain "retry" and an agent will resend a malformed id three times.

That is why the payload also carries retryWith: same_input, corrected_input or never. If you keep only the boolean to match the exam's wording, make sure the message for a validation error names the field and the expected format. Then the model's retry is a corrected one.
a8bcaffcb1:
Once the categories are fixed, the payload is a small API design problem with an unusual consumer. It has four requirements.

  • It must be short, because it is resent in the history on every later turn, like any tool result (chapter 01, section 07).
  • It must be precise enough to branch on, because the model's next step depends on it.
  • It must not leak, because everything in it can end up in front of a customer.
  • It must be stable, because prompts, hooks and tests will come to depend on its field names.

The companion code settles on the following fields. Each is there for a reason that the next table spells out, and the first three are the exam's.
0eb7f5e90d:
A contract is only a contract if something checks it. Example 04 puts a JSON Schema in front of every payload the server can produce. The conditional clauses are the important part. A business error without a customerMessage is invalid. A non-retryable transient error (an unknown write outcome) must carry outcomeUnknown and a nextStep.

Add a leak scan over the same payloads: stack traces, internal hostnames, SQL fragments, secret-like assignments, and the phrase pattern "belongs to another customer". Run both in CI, and the common regressions are caught before the model ever sees them.
9feebc5108:
Three rules, each from a real incident class.

Never leak internals. A message such as "could not connect to db-prod-7.internal:5432" tells an attacker your topology. It tells a curious customer too, via the model's reply. And it tells the model nothing it can act on. The SDK behaviour in section 03 is the cautionary tale: one SDK generation leaks it by default. Put the detail in your server log under the requestId, and put "the order service is unavailable" in the message.

Never confirm what the caller may not know. "Order ORD-118204 belongs to another customer" confirms that the order exists and who owns it. The companion server answers "No order ORD-118204 on this account", which is identical to the answer for an id that does not exist anywhere.

Do not tell the model to promise anything. "Your refund will arrive in 3 days" in a payload becomes a commitment the model repeats. Put facts in the message, and let policy text live in customerMessage, where it is reviewed.
ab3a2f4f46:
Where does the JSON go? In the text content block of the result.

MCP also defines structuredContent (and an optional outputSchema) for typed results. The spec says a tool that returns structured content SHOULD also return the serialised JSON in a text block, for compatibility. Whether a given host forwards structuredContent to the model, rather than only the content blocks, is host behaviour you should check. The safe design puts the full payload in text and treats structuredContent as an addition for programmatic clients.
4d96846808:
The exam statement is short: returning non-retryable errors as retryable wastes calls. The engineering behind it is larger, because "retry" is not one thing.

A failed call can be repeated in three places. Each has different information and a different cost of being wrong. Let all three retry independently and the load on the dependency multiplies, at exactly the moment it is struggling. Design the ownership of retries before you design any single retry.
efa8738d50:
The companion code follows the ownership rule you'd use for a Spring service calling a flaky dependency, with a third party added.

  • The adapter inside the tool retries transient blips once or twice with jittered backoff. It knows the call is idempotent and can hide the blip entirely.
  • The harness (or the subagent loop) reads isRetryable and retryAfterSeconds from an isError result. It retries a plain transient failure within a budget of attempts and of elapsed time, and logs each retry.
  • The model does not retry transient failures blindly. Its job starts where retrying ends: choose an alternative, ask the customer, or report the gap.

For idempotency of reads, that is the whole story. For writes there is one more case.
962923bcd8:
Write the harness side as an explicit state machine, so every outcome is named and testable.

Only one path loops: a transient, retryable failure with budget left. Everything else leaves the loop, and each exit has a different next owner. A validation error, a business error and a permission error return to the model, because only the model (or a human) can change the input, explain the policy or escalate. An unknown outcome on a write goes to a status check. An exhausted budget returns the last failure to the model, with the attempts recorded.
37fef187b1:
Two details in that code deserve a sentence each.

Honour Retry-After, but not blindly. A 30-second wait on a 20-second budget should end the attempt immediately and return the failure. A customer on a chat will not wait. And the model can do something useful with the answer "unavailable for 30 seconds" (tell the customer, offer a callback) that it cannot do while the harness is sleeping.

Jitter. When a dependency recovers, a hundred clients that all retry at exactly 0.5 seconds arrive together and knock it over again. Full jitter spreads them out: a random wait between zero and the exponential ceiling, the variant from the AWS Architecture Blog's 2015 article on backoff. Example 05 prints five clients with and without it.
53caf165a7:
A read timeout is a clean failure: nothing happened, so repeat it. A write timeout is not. The client sent "refund 45.00 on ORD-305519", the service did it, and the response was lost. A retry now refunds twice.

Example 07 takes the same fault through three strategies.

  • A: retry with a fresh idempotency key. It looks like a new refund, so you get two refunds.
  • B: retry with the same idempotency key. The backend returns the original refund with replayed: true. One refund.
  • C: read the error, see outcomeUnknown, call a status tool for the order, and retry only if nothing exists. One refund, and it works even when the backend does not support idempotency keys.

The tool in the companion code marks that timeout isRetryable: false plus outcomeUnknown: true, and names the status tool in nextStep. A model can't mistake it for a blip.
007242f8a7:
Everything above assumes the model heeds isRetryable: false. Usually it does. But a harness for a system where a repeated call has a real cost (a payment, a SIM swap, a port-out) should not rely on usually.

A retry guard remembers calls that failed non-retryably: business, permission, or an unknown write outcome. It answers an identical repetition locally with a structured refusal, so the dependency never sees it. A call with different arguments, a corrected one, is not blocked. This is the same division of labour as chapter 03. The model proposes; the harness enforces what must always hold.
a5e32bbf94:
A business error ends with words said to a person. The question is who writes them.

If the tool returns only a system-vocabulary message, the model has to translate it. Translation is where it improvises. It softens a firm policy into a maybe, hardens a discretionary one into a no, or invents an alternative the business does not offer.

If the tool carries the sentence, the policy owner wrote it and legal reviewed it. The model's job shrinks to choosing when to say it and fitting it into the conversation. The exam skill is "customer-friendly explanations for non-retryable business errors". The design decision behind it is that the tool is the source of truth about policy, because it is the component that enforced the policy.
e1556589bc:
Example 08 puts three versions of the same refusal through the same reader.

V1 has only a system message. The reader relays "Sorry, I can't do that: RULE_RW30 violated: delivered_on(2026-08-24) + 30d < today(2026-10-08); status=INELIGIBLE_WINDOW". V2 adds a customerMessage ("This order is outside our 30-day refund window."). The reply is now correct, but it leaves the customer at a dead end. V3 adds alternatives and a message that offers them ("I can offer store credit or connect you with a specialist"). Now the model has something to do next. A CI contract test over every business error the server can raise catches V1 and V2:
57fbea73aa:
Two refinements.

First, permission errors that the customer can resolve (verify your identity) benefit from the same treatment. The companion server gives the over-limit refund a customerMessage ("Refunds of this size need a supervisor's approval. I'll pass your case to one now.") and a nextStep that names the escalation tool. So the model both says the right thing and does the right thing.

Second, the model keeps its latitude over tone and sequencing. With customerMessage in hand, it can acknowledge the customer's frustration first. It can combine two failures from one turn into one coherent reply. What it should not do is rewrite the policy.

Suppose your evaluation finds the model paraphrasing the policy in ways that change its meaning. The fix is a system prompt line telling it to relay the customerMessage faithfully, plus the contract test above. A longer message won't fix it. Chapter 14 covers when a business error should end in escalation rather than an explanation.
cd38359175:
This is the one error-handling bug that makes no noise. A tool can't reach its data and returns an empty list. It has just converted a failure into a statement about the world. The model has no other source, so it repeats that statement as fact.

Nothing in the logs distinguishes it from a customer who really has no orders. No exception, no error flag, a fluent reply.

The rule fits in one line, and it belongs in every read tool: an empty result means the query ran and found nothing; anything that stopped the query from running is an error. Example 09 shows what each design says to the same question, "What orders do I have?", when the first call to the order service times out.
a434201e12:
The third column is why a boolean is not enough. Many systems filter results silently. Row-level security hides what the caller cannot read. A search index lags by an hour. A pagination cursor expires after the first page. A downstream shard is down, and the aggregator returns what the other shards had. In each case "the list I returned" is not "the list".

The remedy is to make the scope part of the result: searched_days, complete, and, when complete is false, an omitted_reason the model can relay or act on. With those, even a result that looks like success carries its own caveat.

For lookups by id, the same logic gives two outcomes the tool should keep distinct. found: false for "that id does not exist" is a valid answer to "does this order exist". An id that is not even well formed is a validation error, because a corrected id could succeed.
b96e9cf69f:
Test this property rather than relying on review. The contract suite (example 24) injects a timeout into every read tool. It asserts that the result is an error and does not contain the success field (orders). Then it asks the same tool for a range that has no data and asserts complete: true, count: 0, and searched_days as requested.

Chapter 15 carries the same distinction across agents. A subagent that cannot search must say so, not return an empty findings list. Otherwise the final report asserts that nothing exists.
b35268d69f:
In a coordinator and subagent system (chapter 02), the coordinator never sees the subagent's tool calls. It sees what the subagent returns. That makes the subagent the right place to absorb everything it can fix, and the return value the place to put everything it cannot.

The principle is the one you apply to a service chain. Handle a failure at the lowest level that has the information and authority to handle it, and let only the residue travel up. A timeout on one of five searches is fixed by a retry and costs the coordinator nothing. A permission failure on the archive is not the subagent's to fix, so it goes up at once. The coordinator's context stays free for decisions that need it, and it decides with accurate facts about what is left.
b8449f3fe4:
The return value carries the structure chapter 15 develops: a failure_type (timeout, permission_denied, invalid_query, source_unavailable), the attempted query or operation, any partial results, alternatives, and a coverage summary.

This chapter's errorCategory is the tool-level vocabulary. failure_type is the agent-level one. The subagent translates one into the other when it decides a failure cannot be resolved locally. That translation is where the category earns its keep:

  • a transient failure that exhausted its retries becomes timeout or source_unavailable;
  • a permission failure becomes permission_denied and is never retried;
  • a validation failure that the subagent could not repair becomes invalid_query;
  • a business failure becomes a blocked-by-policy failure, with the customerMessage and alternatives intact.
8ae72ddf1f:
Compare the wrong shapes the official guide warns about. Each one corresponds to a line you could have written.

  • A generic status ("search unavailable") leaves the coordinator unable to choose between retrying, re-delegating and annotating.
  • Silent suppression (return an empty findings list for q4 and q5) makes the final report claim that nothing exists on those topics.
  • Terminating the whole workflow on the first failure throws away the three queries that worked.
  • Unbounded local retry burns minutes on a failure that will never clear, and the coordinator never learns it is happening.

Local recovery is bounded by the same attempts-and-time budget as any retry. An unrecovered failure is reported, not swallowed.
d1e5732e68:
The pieces so far assemble into a small server. The file header states its four design rules:

  1. a failure is a result with isError: true, never a swallowed exception and never an empty success;
  2. the body is JSON with the category, the retry verdict and the message, plus the extras the category needs;
  3. anticipated failures are ToolFailure, and anything else is caught by the decorator and reported as internal with a generic message and a request id;
  4. reads distinguish an empty answer from a failed search.

The decorator is the whole mechanism. It's also where the SDK differences from section 03 stop mattering, because nothing reaches the framework as an exception.
989587ca6a:
Four things in that code deserve attention.

The docstring is the tool description (chapter 05), and it documents the error contract. That includes the unusual case (outcomeUnknown) and the idempotency-key rule. Without it, the field names are a private convention the model has to guess.

The annotations are MCP's tool hints: readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint and openWorldHint. The spec is explicit that clients must treat them as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server. So they inform a host's prompts and permissions, but enforce nothing.

The same order read serves "missing" and "someone else's", so the error does not leak ownership.

And every branch raises. No branch builds a result by hand, so a new branch can't forget the structure.
7d47696a3d:
Argument validation deserves its own warning, because it happens before your decorator runs. Declare amount_usd: float, and the SDK validates the argument against the generated schema. On failure it answers with its own message (a pydantic validation text in an isError result), and your code never runs.

That's a perfectly good error for a model to correct from. But it is not your contract: no category, no field name.

Example 12 shows both, plus the alternative: declare the parameter loosely (amount: float | str) and validate inside the tool. That costs a little schema precision and buys one uniform format. Whether the trade is worth it depends on how much of your prompting and hooks depend on the fields. For a payments tool, the uniformity usually wins.
34f7163816:
To use the server from Claude Code, register it and let the host namespace it. claude mcp add orders -- python orders_server.py exposes the tools as mcp__orders__lookup_order and so on. That is also how you list them in a subagent's tools (section 15). Chapter 07 covers the configuration scopes and the project .mcp.json.

The examples never need a subprocess. mcp_compat.connect(server) opens an in-memory client session, which is also how the contract tests in section 20 run.
d88f2c597f:
The schema comments in the MCP specification are the final word on why the decorator exists. The CallToolResult definition says: "Any errors that originate from the tool SHOULD be reported inside the result object, with isError set to true, not as an MCP protocol-level error response. Otherwise, the LLM would not be able to see that an error occurred and self-correct." For the other channel, errors in finding the tool, or a server that does not support tool calls, "should be reported as an MCP error response".

One consequence is worth testing in your SDK. Per that comment, an unknown tool name is a protocol error. Yet both SDK generations here return it as an isError result. Either is survivable if your host passes it to the model. Just don't write code that depends on which.
beb515542b:
You build tool layers in Java, so the contract should exist in a form you could drop into a Spring service. Nothing about it is Python-specific. It needs a sealed category, one exception type that renders the payload, a classifier for the exceptions your code and libraries already throw, and a retry executor that sends only transient failures round the loop.

The companion java/ErrorTaxonomy.java is a single file with no dependencies. It runs with java ErrorTaxonomy.java on JDK 17 or later, so you can read every piece in one sitting. It renders the same failure two ways: the MCP text payload and an RFC 9457 problem body. In a Spring system, the same business rule often serves both an HTTP API and a tool.
49475f5dd8:
Here are three integration points. They're shown as sketches, because they depend on your Spring version and aren't compiled in the companion folder. Check the reference for your version.

First, an HTTP edge. A @RestControllerAdvice maps ToolFailure to ProblemDetail, with the category and retry verdict as extension properties. Through the classifier, it maps framework exceptions too. A REST client then gets the same information an agent gets, from one implementation of the policy.

Second, retry policy. Resilience4j's RetryConfig takes a predicate over the thrown exception. Point it at the classifier, so that only the transient branch retries, with exponential backoff and jitter. The retry then lives where section 07 said the adapter retry lives.

Third, the tool layer itself. A Java MCP server (the MCP Java SDK, or Spring AI's MCP support) returns a tool result type that has an error flag. The same wrapper that turns exceptions into a payload sits around each tool method. Check the current SDK documentation for the exact result type and builder names; don't rely on a snippet.
d26dfca369:
The mapping between the two worlds is worth stating once. It makes the exam concepts concrete for a Spring reader.

  • A category is an exception hierarchy plus a handler.
  • isRetryable is the predicate you give Resilience4j.
  • customerMessage is the detail you would show an end user, as opposed to the log message.
  • requestId is the trace id in your logs.
  • outcomeUnknown is the reason a payment client never retries a POST without an idempotency key.

And an agent is just a client that reads the body in prose.
80b5b8da95:
The 2.3 claim is that an agent with eighteen tools selects less reliably than one with four or five. The guide gives the reason in one phrase: increased decision complexity.

That phrase is worth unpacking. Four separate mechanisms sit behind it, and they have different remedies. An engineer who knows only the first will "fix" the problem with better descriptions, then be surprised when it persists. The four mechanisms are:

  • more candidates for every decision;
  • more near-duplicates among the candidates;
  • more tokens to read before every decision;
  • more wrong actions available when the decision is wrong.
f03b149022:
Chapter 05 established that there is no router. The tool definitions are rendered into the prompt as text. The model chooses by reading them and emitting a tool_use block.

A choice among five items is a choice among five items. A choice among eighteen is the same operation with thirteen more things that could be mistaken for the right answer. Each of those thirteen is one more place where a customer's phrasing, a keyword in the system prompt, or a similar noun in a description can pull the choice off target. If each one has even a small independent chance of beating the correct tool on some fraction of requests, the error rate grows with the count.

That's a statement about the structure of the problem, not about any particular model. It's why every tool-use guide recommends starting with few tools and adding on evidence, including Anthropic's own guide on writing tools. Their phrasing: more tools do not always lead to better outcomes, and too many tools, or overlapping tools, can distract the agent.
0b8795d0ae:
The count of candidates grows linearly. The count of pairs that could be confused grows with its square. A catalogue of five has ten pairs; eighteen has 153; fifty has 1,225.

In a catalogue grown organically by different people, a fixed fraction of pairs overlap in vocabulary. Two tools mention "customer", three mention "status", four mention "order". So the number of look-alike pairs grows far faster than the number of tools. Chapter 05 gave the screen for finding these pairs. Here the point is the scaling. Section 14 measures it on a pool of fifty return-and-account tools. The expected number of colliding pairs goes from 0 at five tools to 2.7 at eighteen and 32 at fifty.

A team that adds one tool per sprint won't see any single addition make things worse, because each addition adds only a few pairs. The degradation is real, and it's gradual. That's why it usually gets discovered as "the agent got flaky around Q3" rather than as an incident.
85f05a60f9:
Each definition is input the model must process on every request, and the whole list is in play every time. Section 14 puts numbers on the short descriptions used in the simulation: 470 tokens per request at five tools and 3,900 at fifty. That's 39,000 input tokens for a ten-turn task.

Real descriptions are longer than the ones in the simulation. The tool search documentation describes a typical multi-server MCP setup as around 55k tokens of definitions. It states that selection accuracy degrades once you exceed 30 to 50 tools. It gives no source for the number, so read it as vendor guidance, not as a measurement.

Two consequences follow. The money consequence is mild with prompt caching, because definitions sit at the front of the prompt and cache well (the caching section of section 16 says when that stops being true). The attention consequence is not mild. A cached token is still a token the model reads. A list of fifty definitions is fifty paragraphs between the user's question and the model's answer.
3293920cd6:
The first three mechanisms lower accuracy. The fourth raises the price of each error.

Take an agent whose job is to process returns, and which can also see merge_accounts, close_account, update_contact and send_email. It has a lower chance of picking customer_lookup when it should. Worse, when it picks wrong, it can pick wrong in a way that changes data.

The exam's example is a synthesis agent attempting web searches. An agent holding a tool outside its specialty will use it some of the time, because the description looks relevant to something the model is trying to do right now. A web-search tool in the hands of an agent whose contract is "use only what you were given" produces unsourced claims that look sourced. The agent isn't malfunctioning. It's doing what the menu invited.

Writing "do not use web search" in the prompt is not the remedy; that turns a structural problem into a probabilistic one. Take the tool off the menu.
a91ba230fc: Notice what the figure implies for a design review. "Our descriptions are good" defends against only one of four mechanisms. Suppose someone proposes adding a nineteenth tool to a coordinator because the descriptions can carry it. The review question isn't whether the nineteenth description is clear. It's whether the coordinator needs the tool at all, and if not, which agent does.
616f5a82cb:
Claims about "degrades selection reliability" are easy to repeat and hard to feel. So the companion folder measures the shape of the effect.

The honest framing comes first, because it governs how you use the numbers. The selector in these examples is the offline keyword-and-weight scorer from chapter 05, not Claude. It reads the same descriptions and the same user message and picks the best-scoring tool, with a small amount of seeded noise. Its absolute accuracy says nothing about Claude's accuracy, which is far higher on easy requests.

What it can show is the shape. Take the same forty customer requests and a growing pool of tools drawn from a fixed set of fifty. How many requests go to the right tool? How many go to a tool the role should not have, and how many of those are state-changing? The shape follows from the structure of the problem (more competitors). So it's evidence for the mechanism, even though the selector is a stand-in.

Examples 26 and 27 repeat the tool-count run against the real model when a key is available. They were not run for this chapter, so no live numbers appear here.
2db88e182e:
Here's the setup in 13_tool_count_sim.py. A pool of fifty tools has names and descriptions written in the style of a real commerce back office: customer lookup, order search, refunds, shipments, promotions. It also has the neighbours every such system accumulates: merge accounts, update contact, store locator, send email, close account. Five of the tools are the core of a returns role. Forty queries each have one correct core tool.

For each catalogue size N, the example builds many catalogues of N tools. Each always contains the five core tools plus a random draw of the others. It scores every query and reports the mean over draws. The metrics are:

  • "Exact accuracy": the share of queries whose top pick is the correct tool.
  • "Misuse": the share whose top pick is a tool outside the five.
  • "Write misuse": misuse that landed on a state-changing tool.
  • "Contenders": the average number of other tools scoring within 85% of the winner, which counts live alternatives per decision.
1df53041dc:
Read the table behind the figure carefully. It contains two results and an inconvenient detail.

The first result is the shape. At five tools the proxy is at its ceiling for this query set (92.5%). Every added tool can only add contenders, so accuracy can't rise and mostly falls. The number of live contenders per decision goes from 0.23 to 0.60.

The second result is that misuse appears from the first additions and grows steadily. Three quarters of it lands on tools that change data (7.5 of 10 points at fifty).

The inconvenient detail is that accuracy flattens between 30 and 50 tools (82.4% against 82.5%). That is not evidence that fifty tools are as good as thirty. With a pool of fifty, the N=50 catalogue is always the entire pool, so there's no sampling variation left to average. The 5th-percentile and worst-case columns in the full report show the thirty-tool catalogues with wide spread. The sensible reading is "the curve is flat-ish once many look-alikes are already present". That's the shape you'd expect when the confusable pairs are already in.
afe58355a7:
The aggregate hides the mechanism, so the example prints the individual misroutes at N=50. Four requests go wrong in a way that matters. In each, the winning tool is one the returns role never needed.

  • "Can you find the customer account for sam.lee@example.com?" goes to merge_accounts (score 7.0 against 6.8 for the correct customer_lookup). The word "account" appears in the merge description more often than in the lookup description.
  • "I lost my account number, the contact on file is 201-555-0123" goes to update_contact by a wide margin (16.7 to 10.5), because "contact" is in the tool's name.
  • "Find my customer record using priya.n@example.com" goes to store_locator, a read-only tool that returns nothing useful.
  • "Yes, go ahead and send the money back for ORD-305519 to my card" goes to send_email, because "send" dominates.

None of these descriptions is bad. Each is a perfectly good description of a different tool. The failure is that the tool was on the menu.
fd996f0db9:
Now the control experiment. A skeptic should ask whether better descriptions would erase the effect. The example repeats the run with "fenced" descriptions: each description in the pool gets a sentence naming the neighbour it should not be used for.

The result is nearly identical: 84.7% against 84.5% at eighteen tools, 82.5% against 82.5% at fifty. Fencing helps where the fence names the vocabulary that actually collides. It does nothing where it doesn't. And in a pool of fifty there are far too many collision points to fence by hand.

Compare the last experiment in the example, which isn't a description change at all. Give the agent the role catalogue of five tools, and ask the same questions in the same pool context. Exact accuracy is 95.0%, and out-of-role picks are 0%.

Scoping did not make the descriptions better. It removed the candidates that could not be right. That's the whole argument for 2.3 in one comparison.
40eb0af5b3:
It cannot tell you where Claude's own accuracy falls off. A current model separates well-written tools far better than a keyword scorer does. Where degradation becomes visible depends on the model, the descriptions and the traffic. Nor can it tell you that 18 is bad and 5 is good; those are the exam's illustrative numbers.

What you can take from it is this. The direction is structural. The cost of out-of-role tools is a misuse rate, not only an accuracy figure. And the way to learn about your own system is to run the evaluation harness from chapter 05 at your catalogue sizes. Examples 26 and 27 do this against the live model.
3f063d1db1:
The remedy has three parts, and the exam teaches them in the order an architect would apply them.

  1. Give each agent only the tools its role needs.
  2. Where a role needs a capability that a generic tool provides, give it a constrained version that can't do what the role must not do.
  3. Where a role keeps needing something that belongs to another role, and the need is frequent and simple, give it a narrow tool for exactly that need. Don't route every instance through a coordinator.

Skipping straight to the third is the common mistake. It fixes the visible latency and brings back the original problem with a smaller footprint.
a9a312fd57:
In a multi-agent system built on the Claude Agent SDK, the coordinator and its subagents are defined in code or configuration. The tool set is part of each definition. The subagent definition has a tools field that lists what that subagent may use.

If you leave tools out, the subagent inherits every tool the parent has. For a parent configured with the whole kitchen, that's the least-privilege failure in its purest form. It happens by omission, nothing in the code looks wrong, and the first sign is a synthesis agent running a web search.

There's also a disallowedTools field. It removes tools from whatever pool the agent would otherwise get, and it's applied first. That's the useful form when the pool is "everything except".

MCP tools are named mcp__<server>__<tool>. The configuration accepts the mcp__<server> prefix as a way to grant a whole server. But granting a whole server to a role that needs one of its tools repeats the omission mistake one level down, so prefer tool names.

(Field and pattern names are as in the Claude Code subagent documentation and the installed Agent SDK types at the time of writing. The documentation has recently renamed the delegation tool from Task to Agent, so check the docs for your version.)
ff9cc02efc:
The companion example 17_scoped_tool_sets.py keeps the role matrix as data and checks it. Printed as a matrix:

  • the coordinator holds only the delegation tool;
  • the web researcher holds the two web tools;
  • the document analyst holds one grep and one internal fetch;
  • the synthesizer holds the scoped fact checker and the report saver.

The validator reports the definition tokens each role pays: 250, 380, 300 and 290, against 2,260 for every role when everyone gets everything. It then runs against a deliberately broken configuration and flags the three classic faults. A read-only role holds Bash. A role's tools is omitted, so it inherits the parent's. A coordinator holds more than the delegation tool.

The practical rule: the role matrix belongs in version control next to the agent definitions, and CI checks it. A tool list that changes by accident is configuration drift, not a code change anyone reviews.
3e797d3a65:
A generic tool (fetch_url, run_sql, bash) is flexible because it takes an unconstrained argument. For the same reason, it's the tool a role most often misuses. Its description has to be generic, which makes it match almost any request. And its argument space includes the dangerous cases.

The exam's example is replacing fetch_url with load_document that validates the URL. The general rule: for every role, ask what it needs to do, then offer a tool whose parameters can express only that.

The companion's 19_constrained_replacements.py runs five hostile probes against both shapes. The generic fetch executes all of them. That includes the cloud metadata address 169.254.169.254, a file:///etc/passwd read, an arbitrary external host with a query string, and localhost:8080/actuator/env. The allowlisted fetch refuses four of the five with a permission error (only https, only approved hosts) and executes the legitimate one.

A document tool that takes a doc_id of the form DOC-12345 refuses a path traversal as a validation error, and a missing id as a validation error too. The SQL pair makes the same point. run_sql executes DELETE FROM orders and a stacked DROP TABLE. orders_by_status(status, max_age_days) takes an enum and a bounded integer, and can express neither.
6ce4cec8b4:
Two details are easy to miss.

First, the constrained tool's refusal message names where to go instead. That's the error-payload habit from section 06, applied to scope. A model stopped by a permission error with no next step will often retry with a variation.

Second, the constrained tool is a better guarantee than any prompt text. "The model followed the instruction" is a probability. "The tool cannot do it" is a fact.

The costs are real: one more tool definition to write and maintain per role, and a refusal path to test. They're small against the cost of the first incident.
04937cffc6:
Scoping creates a coordination cost, and the exam makes it explicit. Say the synthesis agent needs to check a date or a figure while writing, and it has no search tool. Every check then goes back to the coordinator, which delegates to the web agent, which searches, and the answer returns through the coordinator to the synthesis agent. In a hub-and-spoke system, that's two extra model round trips per check.

The official sample (Q9) gives the numbers. The synthesis agent needs simple fact checks in 85% of its tasks, and each costs a round trip that adds 40% to the total latency. The other 15% are complex verifications that should go through the coordinator. The right answer in the guide gives the synthesis agent a scoped verify_fact for the simple checks, and keeps routing the complex ones through the coordinator.

The alternatives are instructive. (I'm not reproducing the sample's exact option wording; these are the natural competitors.)

  • Giving the synthesis agent the full web toolset solves the latency by removing the scoping that was the point.
  • Having it batch its checks to the end removes a dependency, but lets the report be built on unchecked facts.
  • Speculatively pre-verifying every claim wastes searches on claims nobody needs, and still misses the unanticipated ones.
33c16dab30:
The companion's 18_verify_fact_q9.py models each design with a small latency simulation. It prints every parameter so you can change them. The baseline is 100 seconds for a report with no fact checks. Each check costs 8 seconds through the coordinator, with five checks per report. The scoped tool is cheap for the 85% and falls back for the rest. The results:

  • the pure-hub design lands at 40% over baseline (140 seconds);
  • the scoped verify_fact design lands at 14% (113.5 seconds);
  • giving the synthesizer the full web tools lands at 30%;
  • pre-verifying every claim lands at 18%, while running about 21 searches against 5;
  • direct agent-to-agent messaging lands at 15%.

The numbers come from the parameters, not from measuring any real system, and they'll change when you change them. The useful output is the structure. The scoped tool removes most of the hub cost without adding a capability the synthesizer shouldn't have.
9b39f6b6a9:
A scoped cross-role tool is only scoped if it refuses what it should not do. If verify_fact will also attempt "why did churn fall at US carriers", the synthesis agent will use it for open-ended research, and the scoping has leaked. So the tool must return an explicit unresolved verdict for anything that isn't a single-fact lookup against a known store, and say where to go.

The example's facts_store.verify_fact returns one of three verdicts:

  • verified, with a value, source and as-of date;
  • unresolved, with reason: "not a single-fact lookup" and route: "needs_research";
  • not_found, with the sources it searched.

The caller's instruction: on needs_research, put the claim in the list returned to the coordinator. That's the guide's "limited cross-role tool" made concrete. Narrow input (an entity and one attribute). Narrow source (a fact store, not the open web). Narrow output. And a refusal path that leads back into the normal architecture.
1b71cd85f6:
Scoping decides which tools are on the menu. tool_choice decides whether the model may decline the menu. It's a parameter on the Messages API request, and it has four forms:

  • {"type": "auto"} is the default when tools are supplied. The model decides whether to call a tool, which one, or to answer in text.
  • {"type": "any"} requires the model to call a tool, but lets it pick which.
  • {"type": "tool", "name": "..."} requires a call to the named tool.
  • {"type": "none"} forbids tool calls even though tool definitions are present. That's useful when you want the model to read the tools (for context in a long conversation, say) but not call them on this turn.

Each of the first three also accepts disable_parallel_tool_use: true, which limits the response to at most one tool call. none has no parallelism to disable, and the type definitions in the Python SDK agree.

The parameter lives on the request, not on the conversation or the tool. So it can change between turns. Both the forced-first-tool pattern and its main limitation come from that fact.
e532d066d6:
The mechanism behind any and tool is documented as prefill. The API effectively starts the assistant turn with the beginning of a tool call, so the model can't write any text before it. You can see two consequences in the contract checker in 20_tool_choice_semantics.py.

The first concerns narration. Under auto, a response may contain a text block and a tool_use block, with the model explaining what it's about to do. Under any and tool, the response begins with the tool_use. Any "I will look that up for you" narration is gone, and it isn't available for a log or a user interface. A design that depends on the narration should use auto and enforce the call some other way.

The second concerns caching. The docs state that changing tool_choice invalidates cached message blocks, while the cached tool definitions and system prompt stay valid. The example's simulator reports one invalidation of the conversation prefix when a conversation alternates between forced and automatic turns. An agent that flips tool_choice on every turn pays to reprocess its history each time.
c2ee7acd7c:
Two restrictions matter enough to design around. Both were true of the documentation at the time of writing, so verify them for your model before you rely on them.

First, extended thinking. With manual extended thinking enabled (thinking.type = "enabled"), the API rejects any and tool with an error. Only auto and none work with it. The reason: forcing a tool call by prefill leaves no room for the thinking that precedes it. The docs say adaptive thinking does not itself block forced tool use, so the two cases differ; check the docs for the combination you use. The simulator encodes the rule. It shows the 400 with the message "Thinking may not be enabled when tool_choice forces tool use.", while auto with thinking passes.

Second, model support. The docs table listed some current models as returning a 400 for any and tool, including the Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 generations this guide's examples assume. It recommended auto together with strict tool use or structured outputs instead. If that holds for your model, forcing is no longer an available lever for it, and sections 17 and 18 give the replacements.

I could not verify the whole model matrix from here. The table changes with model releases, so look it up for the model ID you deploy. Then write a test that fails when the behaviour changes.
2f3e6fb102:
A third point is a common source of confusion rather than a restriction. tool_choice applies to one request. It forces the next response to contain a call. It doesn't persist. It says nothing about the response after the tool result comes back. And it doesn't stop the model from calling other tools in later turns.

A forced call also doesn't validate the arguments beyond the tool's schema. The model can put plausible nonsense in the required fields. If the schema has no "none of the above" option, the nonsense is the only thing it can do. Both facts matter in the next two sections.
ba2699088e:
The official sample pattern is to force a specific tool to run first. Their example is extract_metadata before any enrichment step. The pipeline must know the document type before it can choose what to do next. Leave that to the model's judgement, and on some fraction of requests it will skip the step.

With tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} on the first request, the response is a call to that tool, with arguments the model fills in from the document. After the tool result is appended, the next request returns to auto, so the model can continue the loop. The skill being tested is that the force is for turn one only. Leave a force in place and the model calls the same tool forever.
5f2c21d315:
It's easy to hear "force extract_metadata first" as "extract_metadata always runs before anything else". It doesn't say that. It says the first response contains that call.

Look at what the second turn is allowed to do. The first tool's result is on the table, and tool_choice is back at auto. The model can call process_refund whether or not the first result was a success.

Example 21_forced_first_tool.py shows this with a refund flow where verification is get_customer. In variant A, the first turn is forced to get_customer. The customer lookup fails (a wrong email, a validation error). On turn two the scripted model reads the error as noise and calls process_refund, which succeeds: RF-UNGATED. The force did its job, and the refund still went out unverified. The bug isn't in the force. It's in the assumption that the force enforces order.
8010cc24ac:
Variant B adds the prerequisite check inside process_refund. The tool asks the session store whether the session has a verified customer. If not, it returns a permission error: not retryable, with the next step "verify the customer first".

The same flow now ends with the refund refused and the reason in the model's context. On the happy path (right email), the refund goes through, so the check costs nothing when the sequence is right.

That's the pattern: force is the nudge, the server-side check is the rule. It's the same split chapter 01 drew between prompt-level guidance and programmatic enforcement. And it's the one the exam rewards when the stakes are financial or identity-related.
ab78e1ef35:
Variant C reaches the same ordering without tool_choice at all. It's the fallback for models that reject forced selection. On the first request, offer only get_customer; on later requests, offer the full list. There's no instruction to follow and no parameter to reject. The second tool simply doesn't exist yet on turn one.

The costs are different. Changing the tools list changes the front of the cached prefix. So it invalidates more cache than changing tool_choice does (the docs describe the cache hierarchy; measure on your traffic). And a conditional tool list is a state machine you now own. For a two-step flow with a cheap first request, that's usually fine. For a long flow with a big system prompt, the cached prefix may matter more than the elegance.
7d2f03e94d:
The third form, any, answers a different question. Not "which tool first?" but "must this response be a tool call?". Two uses are standard.

The first is routing. A triage step that must pick one of several handlers can't be allowed to answer in prose. So you define each handler as a tool and set tool_choice: any.

The second is structured output, an idiom that predates dedicated structured-output features. Define a tool whose input schema is the object you want, force a call, and read the arguments out of the tool_use block as the result. The response is never parsed from prose, and the schema constrains its shape.
c14667c39c:
The exam's trap is that the schema constrains the shape and nothing else. Example 22_any_structured_routing.py gives a classifier three extraction tools (extract_invoice, extract_contract, and so on) and forces any. An invoice and a contract go to the right tool and produce valid output.

A marketing email is neither, but it still has to call something, because any forbids a text reply. The scripted model picks extract_invoice and fills it with invoice_id: "UNKNOWN", total: 0. That validates against the schema, and it's false. No error was raised and no log line looks odd. Yet a downstream system now holds an invoice that doesn't exist.

This is the structured-output version of the empty-versus-failure problem in section 09: a successful-looking result that really means "I had no honest answer".
cb858d35a4:
Three more points complete the picture.

First, a document nested in a larger conversation sometimes needs a different shape on each of several turns. With any on every turn, the model can never produce a text answer for the user. Use it for the extraction request, and switch back to auto for the conversational one, mindful of the caching cost of switching.

Second, on models where any is rejected, the docs offer two options. One is strict tool use with auto, which gives schema-conformant arguments whenever the model does call a tool. The other is the structured-output feature, which is a response format, not a tool call. Both guarantee shape. Neither guarantees that a call happens, and the exit-tool principle applies equally.

Third, for output you'll parse in Java, the schema is also a contract your own code can check. Model it as a record with a sealed hierarchy for the three shapes plus the exit. Then the downstream code can't compile a path that forgets the "none of these" case.
9db97e56d1:
So far each piece was shown alone. Example 23_end_to_end_agent.py puts them in one run, so you can see where each one acts.

The server (the same orders_server.py as section 11) exposes four tools. The returns role is allowed three of them; search_orders belongs to a different role. The harness wraps the MCP session in a dispatcher that does three things around each call:

  • it refuses a tool name outside the role, with a structured validation error that lists the allowed names;
  • it retries transient failures with bounded exponential backoff and jitter, on a fake clock;
  • it passes everything else to the model unchanged.

The first request carries tool_choice forcing lookup_order, on a model that accepts it. Every later request is auto. The model is a script, and it makes one mistake on purpose: on turn two it calls search_orders, a tool the role does not have.
12aff10ddd:
Read the trace in order. Turn one is the forced call, and the order comes back. On turn two the model drifts to search_orders. Nothing breaks. The dispatcher returns a validation error that lists the tools the role does have, and the model reads it. On turn three it calls process_refund with a correct amount, and the refund is created exactly once.

The stats line gives the accounting. Three tool calls reached the server. One transient fault was retried by the harness, so the model never saw it. One out-of-scope call was absorbed.

Note what a real deployment would also have. The tool list sent to the model on every request is the role list. So the drift above couldn't happen for a role-scoped agent unless the model invented the name. This example sends the model a script that does exactly that. The point is to show that a stale or hallucinated tool name is handled as an ordinary recoverable failure, not as an exception that ends the run.
a24d443178:
Both halves of this chapter fail silently. A uniform error looks like an error. A leaky tool list looks like a working agent. Neither shows in a demo, and both show in production a few weeks later.

The defence is to write the contracts down as tests that run on every build. That's possible because every claim in the chapter is about structure, not about model behaviour. Example 24_contract_tests.py is such a suite (19 tests, all offline, 0.2 seconds). Read it as a checklist of what to assert for any tool server you own.
716e7f6dca: Every failure is an isError result with the required fields (errorCategory, isRetryable, message). That includes the framework-generated ones you didn't write, such as argument validation and unknown tool. The test fires a representative failure of each kind and checks the shape. It's the test that catches a new tool added without the decorator.
5ae8076974: No two different failures share the same message. This is the "no uniform errors" test. The messages produced by timeout, bad id, policy refusal and missing permission form a set with four distinct members.
10617862f8: No internal detail leaks: a regular expression runs over every error body, looking for stack traces, .internal hostnames, SQL keywords and the text "belongs to another" (the cross-account case). That last one is a security test. A customer's order id that belongs to someone else must look identical to one that does not exist.
e43a78a053: The tool_choice contract: any and tool drop leading text. A forced call with manual thinking is a 400. The 5.5 models reject forced selection (until the docs say otherwise, and the test is what tells you). none forbids calls.
a27b25aa13: Monotone sanity checks on the simulation: out-of-role picks are zero with the role catalogue and positive with the whole pool. A change that breaks the simulation then fails loudly, instead of printing a believable table.
4bf1f4cba8:
Two of these deserve a comment.

The "no internal detail" test exists because the Python MCP SDK's behaviour changed between major versions. 1.x returned the text of an uncaught exception to the client; 2.x returns a generic "Error executing tool X". Example 12 shows both. A server written against 1.x that relied on an exception message to inform the model works until the SDK upgrade. The reverse holds too: a server that relied on 1.x's leak for debugging gets an unhelpful error after the upgrade. Putting the shape of the error under a test makes the behaviour independent of the SDK version.

The suite includes the cross-account case because the most dangerous structured errors are the helpful ones. "This order belongs to a different customer" is a data leak, and the structured form makes it easy to say by accident.
b72823e48e: Once the contract is in production, the questions change. "Is it correct?" becomes "is it still correct, and where is it eroding?". Example 25_observability.py runs 300 simulated calls with seeded faults. It writes one structured log line per call and computes the metrics below. The point of the numbers is which ones to alert on, not their values.
1a7cd2f07f:
Five signals earn a place on a dashboard.

  • isError without a category is the uniform error returning, usually from a new tool or an upgraded SDK. Its alert threshold is zero.
  • The internal-category rate is your bug rate. Internal means the tool raised something you didn't anticipate, and a rise after a deploy is a regression.
  • The transient share and its retry count tell you about a dependency. The retry-amplification ratio (attempts divided by logical calls, summed across the layers) tells you whether your retries protect the dependency or lean on it. A ratio near the product of the layer limits (27 in the section 07 example) means a retry storm.
  • Empty results per tool, against the transient rate is the swallowed-failure detector. If a search tool returns empties at the same time its dependency is failing, some failure is being reported as nothing.
  • Calls outside the role is the tool-scope detector. If an agent calls a tool that isn't in its role, either the scope is wrong or the model is inventing names. Both are worth knowing.

In the simulation, 21% of calls fall outside the returns role, because the script exercises search_orders. In a deployed system that figure should be near zero for a scoped agent.
4fe40ae892:
The join key is requestId. The tool generates it, puts it in the error payload, and logs it. The model may quote it back in a hand-off, and that lets a person find the log line for a failure the model reports.

Latency belongs on the same line. "Transient with 30-second latency" and "transient with 30-millisecond latency" are different incidents. In a Spring service, the same line comes from the @RestControllerAdvice or the MCP tool wrapper, through the logging context (MDC). It's the same entry you'd already index for HTTP.
b8b4981843:
The offline examples show that a design is consistent. They can't show that Claude behaves as the scripted reader does. Examples 26 and 27 close that gap when you have an API key.

  • 26_live_tool_count.py sends the forty queries to the real model with catalogues of increasing size. It compares exact accuracy and out-of-role picks with the proxy's.
  • 27_live_error_reading.py gives the real model a tool that fails with a uniform error, then a structured one. It counts retries of non-retryable errors and wrong customer-facing messages.

Both skip cleanly without a key. They weren't run for this chapter, so there are no live numbers in it. Run them first, before relying on any threshold from this chapter.

Example 28_retry_guard.py shows the harness-side guard. It suppresses an identical repeated call after a non-retryable error (the "model retries a business error with the same input" failure). You can see how it reduces wasted calls when the model ignores the flag.
e8d8281dfa: The anti-patterns below have already appeared in context elsewhere in the chapter. This section collects them as a review checklist. Each comes with the symptom you'd see, the broken code or configuration, and the fix. The code for the first three is in sections 06 to 09; here it appears in its smallest form.
f97f589043: Symptom: the agent retries policy refusals, apologises for outages that were really permission problems, or gives up on timeouts. In example 02, across three failures, the blind reader causes 8 upstream order lookups against the structured reader's 4. It also answers two of the three wrongly. Section 04 has the trace.
6cdc296a14:
The scenario questions for 2.2 and 2.3 reward the same habit. Find the layer where the fault actually is before you choose a fix. For errors, that layer is the tool's response. For tool distribution, it's the agent's tool list.

Decide your answer before reading the reasoning. The scenarios are written in the style of the exam, and the options are mine unless stated. The official Q9 is reconstructed from the sample's description.
abf888169c:
The fault is in the response. A failure was delivered as an ordinary result with no category, so the coordinator couldn't tell a timeout from an empty search.

B fixes it where it starts. The local retry means the coordinator only hears about failures that persisted. A is a prompt patch for information the coordinator doesn't have. C builds a string-matching retry that will retry non-transient failures that happen to include the word. D is the worst of the four. It makes the access failure indistinguishable from a valid empty result, which is the exact problem.
8b3d3ea962:
It's a policy violation. The request is understood and forbidden, so retrying is wasted effort and splitting is evasion. The category and the flag stop the retry. The customer-facing wording lets the agent explain. The alternative gives it somewhere to go.

B invites exactly the split the limit exists to prevent. C converts a refusal into a false success, and the customer expects money that will not arrive. D reports a failure of the work as a failure of the protocol. There the model typically never sees it, so it can't reply sensibly.
1c4efbbb31:
Information is destroyed at the tool, so it has to be preserved at the tool. B keeps an access failure distinct from a valid empty result, and makes the valid empty result say what it covers.

A relies on a model to detect something it can't see. C adds a second place for the same swallowing to happen. D changes the question.
2d2563fcf6:
A applies the narrow cross-role tool. It removes the round trips for the 85%, and leaves the 15% where oversight and error handling live.

B resolves the latency by dissolving the separation. The synthesis agent becomes a researcher with web access, and its prompt now competes with that. C removes the latency per check, but lets the report be built on unchecked facts, and adds a final step that can invalidate the document. D spends searches on claims nobody asked about, and still has hub trips for claims it didn't anticipate. The simulation in section 15 puts it at 20.8 searches against 5. (Option wording is reconstructed; the structure is the sample's.)
fe9b5b96ce:
The problem is decision complexity, plus out-of-role misuse that can write data. B removes candidates, look-alike pairs, tokens and blast radius together.

A treats one mechanism of four. It also adds a keyword-laden instruction that can itself skew selection (chapter 05, section 12). C forces a call, which makes the wrong call mandatory when no tool is right. D changes packaging, not the number of tools the model must weigh.
209b659687:
The force guarantees turn one. The server check guarantees the order afterwards, including when the first call fails.

A is a probabilistic fix for a probabilistic fault, and a keyword-heavy instruction too (section 12 of chapter 05). C makes the model call the same tool forever. D guarantees that some tool is called every turn, which prevents the final text answer. If the model rejects forced selection (check the docs), narrow the tools list for the first request instead.
3587cd1dd8: Run bash run_all.sh. All 28 Python examples and both Java programs should print ok; examples 26 and 27 skip without a key.
5cd7c98310: In 17_scoped_tool_sets.py, give the synthesizer WebSearch. Which validator message fires? Then change the Q9 parameters in 18_verify_fact_q9.py so that the simple share is 50%. At what share does the scoped design lose its advantage over the full toolset?
2da468c8e2:
Done when:

  • you can write the error payload for each of the four categories without looking;
  • you can explain why a write timeout is not simply transient;
  • you can state which statements about tool_choice you have verified against the docs for your model;
  • your CI fails when a tool returns an error without a category, or when an agent's tool list changes.
